title: See Through People's Masks: The Law of Role-playing
coreMove: Read the role a person needs to perform, then compare their second language and repeated behavior with the mask.
sourcePressure: This law says social life runs on performance, and insight comes from reading masks, second language, and the gap between polished presentation and repeated conduct.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Reducing masks to lying instead of seeing ordinary performance, self-protection, and unconscious role needs.

exampleSpecs.domain: a charity gala auctioneer whose warmth spikes only near major donors
exampleSpecs.audience: a board member learning to read performance without moral panic
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether small donors are misread as welcomed when the pattern says otherwise
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the board member marks when the auctioneer's smile appears, disappears, and returns, then connects it to donor status before judging the welcome speech
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a silent-auction bid sheet under a crystal centerpiece

exampleSpecs.domain: a surgical residency interview where an applicant performs humility
exampleSpecs.audience: a program director choosing who can handle correction
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether charm hides contempt for supervision
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director asks about a failed case and watches the applicant's foot tap and blame pattern outpace the polished answer
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a hospital conference table with sealed interview folders

exampleSpecs.domain: a homeowners association meeting led by a neighbor playing peacemaker
exampleSpecs.audience: a resident trying to read why consensus keeps failing
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether hidden control keeps masquerading as civility
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the resident compares three meetings and sees the peacemaker always summarizes dissent into mush before the vote
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stack of printed bylaws clipped with a silver binder clip

exampleSpecs.domain: a competitive baking show contestant praising rivals on camera
exampleSpecs.audience: a producer reading the distance between camera persona and off-camera behavior
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the edit rewards a false role
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the producer predicts the contestant will help a rival, then watches the off-camera ingredient swap refusal reveal the role's limit
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a tray of numbered pastry samples under studio lights

exampleSpecs.domain: a university lab partner who jokes through every mistake
exampleSpecs.audience: a student deciding whether humor is warmth or avoidance
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether data quality suffers because the role never gets named
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the partner spills reagent, makes the same joke, and the student points to the recurring dodge rather than the personality
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a glass pipette rolling toward a taped bench edge

exampleSpecs.domain: a luxury watch salesperson who mirrors every buyer's taste
exampleSpecs.audience: a customer learning to see adaptive performance without feeling flattered
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a costly purchase is driven by reflected identity
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the customer notes the salesperson praised opposite styles to two buyers in ten minutes, then waits before treating the praise as personal insight
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a velvet watch tray under a narrow spotlight

skillTargets: infer the social role a person is protecting

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one polished interaction and note the person's role, their repeated nonverbal leak, and one behavior that either confirms or weakens the mask.

sourceAnchors.name: Milton Erickson
sourceAnchors.detail: the source uses Erickson's attention to mismatches between speech, posture, timing, and tone to ground the second-language method
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Milton Erickson learned to treat a mismatch as a clue, not as instant access to another person's soul.
